subject: Humanities
title: Places and their jobs
objective: Match community places to what people do there.
source_label: CONSTRUCTED TEACHING SOURCE: fictional classroom example, not an archival original.
source_lines: A. Library: borrow books and use information.
B. Health centre: meet a health professional.
C. Bus stop: wait for a bus.
D. Park: use shared outdoor space.
model: I need a book. I choose A, the library.
The place matches the job: borrowing a book.

hinge.question: Which place matches: wait for a bus?
choices: A. Library
B. Bus stop
C. Health centre
hinge.reason: A bus stop is a place to wait for a bus.

task: Match: borrow a book; wait for a bus; meet a nurse.
Choose one place. Complete: People go here to ___.
A visitor wants outdoor space. Choose a place and say why.
answers: Library; bus stop; health centre.
Accept a purpose that matches the selected place.
Park, because it offers shared outdoor space.
exit: Name one place and its job.
misconception: A place can have several uses. Accept a sensible extra use and ask for the reason.
prep: Print the matching pupil sheets. Provide pencils and coloured pencils; pointing or adult scribing is available.

title: Ruth: find the sign of welcome
objective: Name a welcoming action and point to the line that supports it.
source_label: CLASSROOM PARAPHRASE — Ruth 2:8–9 and 14. A short biblical passage, not a complete retelling. The Book of Ruth is in the Jewish Tanakh and Christian Old Testament.
source_lines: R1. Ruth gathers grain left after the harvesters. Boaz asks her to remain near the women in his field.
R2. Boaz tells the men not to trouble Ruth. She may drink the water they have collected.
R3. At mealtime, Boaz invites Ruth to eat. She sits beside the harvesters and has enough food.
model: Claim: Ruth is included at the meal.
Evidence: R3 says Boaz invites her to eat beside the harvesters.

hinge.question: Which claim can we support from these lines?
choices: A. Ruth is invited to eat.
B. Ruth receives wages.
C. Ruth is given a house.
hinge.reason: R3 describes a meal invitation; no line describes wages or a house.

task: Match meal / water / staying near others to R1, R2 or R3.
Choose one action. Complete: Ruth is welcomed when ___. Line ___ shows this.
Check “Ruth was given a paid job.” Mark supported / not shown and explain.
answers: Meal R3; water R2; staying near others R1.
Example: she is invited to eat; R3. Accept another correctly linked action.
Not shown. Gathering grain is described, but wages are not.
exit: Point to one line that shows inclusion. Name the action.
misconception: Gleaning means collecting grain left by harvesters; it does not establish paid employment. Do not add a missing-Ruth scene or invented dialogue.
prep: Print the three numbered lines and response page. Pencil only; no cupboard pack or online playback needed. Read all three lines before discussing.
access: Offer pointing, circling, drawing or scribed answers. Read cards aloud. No personal, family or faith disclosure is required.

subject: Humanities
title: Then and now
objective: Use two dated records to spot change and continuity.
source_label: CONSTRUCTED TEACHING RECORDS: fictional Oak Street; dates are for comparing before and after.
source_lines: Record A - 1980: Oak Street has a library, a bus stop and a small shop.
Record B - 2026: the shop has become a cafe; the library and bus stop remain.
Both records show the same fictional street.
These are written teaching records, not photographs.
model: The shop is in A; the cafe is in B. That is a change.
The library is in both. That is continuity.

hinge.question: Which statement is supported by both records?
choices: A. The library stayed.
B. The street had no buses.
C. Everyone liked the cafe.
hinge.reason: Both dated records include a library. Neither records opinions.

task: Put the two dates in time order.
Find one change and one thing that stayed.
Can the records tell us whether everyone liked the change? Explain or point.
answers: Change: shop became cafe. Stayed: library or bus stop.
No. They describe places, not everyone's opinions.
exit: Tell me one change. Show the clue.
misconception: Do not infer what people felt from a building or a date. Optional approved local photographs extend the exact photo-comparison outcome.
prep: Print the matching pupil sheets. Provide pencils and coloured pencils; pointing or adult scribing is available.

title: Handle it with respect
objective: Choose a respectful action using the object card.
source_label: CONSTRUCTED CLASSROOM DISPLAY — fictional museum cards; these are practice instructions, not universal rules for every faith.
source_lines: O1. Display card: an unlit clay diya, a lamp used by some Hindus at Diwali. The display label says: look only; do not lift this fragile example.
O2. Display card: a paper photograph of the lamp. The label says: handle with clean, dry hands; return it flat.
O3. Before handling: ask permission, read the label, follow its instructions, and return the item carefully.
O4. If the label is missing, pause and ask the responsible adult. Do not guess.
model: The photograph may be handled because O2 permits it.
I keep the fragile lamp on its stand because O1 says look only.

hinge.question: The object label is missing. What is the best next step?
choices: A. Copy how another object was handled.
B. Pause and ask.
C. Pick it up quickly.
hinge.reason: O4 says to ask instead of assuming permission.

task: Sort: lift the fragile lamp / keep the photograph flat / ask when unsure into follow / change.
Write or point to the four checks in O3 in order.
Explain why two items about the same festival have different handling instructions.
answers: Change lifting the lamp; follow keeping the photograph flat and asking.
Ask; read; follow; return.
The fragile lamp and paper photograph are different objects. The label supplies the specific instruction.
exit: Finish: Respect means I will ___ before touching an unfamiliar object.
misconception: Respect does not require sharing a belief. Do not claim that every sacred object needs gloves or has one identical handling rule.
prep: Use the supplied text cards; optionally draw the two objects on the board. No real religious artefact, flame or handling box is required.
access: Offer pointing, circling, drawing or scribed answers. Read cards aloud. No personal, family or faith disclosure is required.

subject: Humanities
title: Same, different, respected
objective: Identify a similarity and a difference without making a guess about someone.
source_label: CONSTRUCTED TEACHING SOURCE: fictional classroom example, not an archival original.
source_lines: Ari and Jo both help at a community garden.
Ari likes drawing signs. Jo likes planting seeds.
Their names do not tell us their beliefs.
Both contributions help the group.
model: Same: both help at the garden.
Different: one draws; one plants. Neither is better.

hinge.question: What can we tell from the card?
choices: A. Both people share one religion.
B. Both help the garden.
C. One person matters less.
hinge.reason: The card says both help; it does not give their religion.

task: Mark one thing the two people share.
Name one difference shown on the card.
Write or say a respectful response to each contribution.
answers: Both help the community garden.
Ari draws signs; Jo plants seeds.
Examples: Your signs help us find things. Your planting helps things grow.
exit: One similarity, one difference, equal respect.
misconception: Never infer beliefs or nationality from names, skin colour or clothing. Use the card, not personal disclosure.
prep: Print the matching pupil sheets. Provide pencils and coloured pencils; pointing or adult scribing is available.

title: Similar actions, different meanings
objective: Identify one similarity and one difference between two source cards.
source_label: CLASSROOM FACT CARDS — short paraphrases of named community sources. These examples do not represent every person in a tradition.
source_lines: D1. At Diwali, many Hindus place small lamps called diyas around homes or places of worship.
D2. Hindu American Foundation describes the light as connected with good overcoming evil and knowledge overcoming ignorance.
C1. At Christmas, Christians celebrate the birth of Jesus.
C2. Church of England worship may use a candle when describing Jesus as the light of the world.
model: Both cards describe using light.
The sources connect that light with different religious meanings.

hinge.question: Both groups use light. What can we conclude?
choices: A. They must have identical beliefs.
B. The action is similar; read each meaning.
C. One festival must be better.
hinge.reason: A shared visible action does not establish an identical belief or a ranking.

task: Underline the object or action using light in D1 and C2.
Complete a two-row grid: festival / source meaning.
Finish: Both ___, but Diwali ___ while the Christmas source ___.
answers: Diyas in D1; a candle in C2.
Diwali: good/knowledge overcoming evil/ignorance. Christmas: Jesus as light of the world.
Example: Both use light, but Diwali links it with good and knowledge while the Christmas source links it with Jesus.
exit: Name a similarity without saying the beliefs are the same.
misconception: Do not turn a source about many people into a claim about everyone. Do not ask pupils to speak on behalf of a religion.
prep: Print the four lines and comparison grid. Pupils may draw a lamp/candle as a learning diagram; no worship action or flame is needed.
access: Offer pointing, circling, drawing or scribed answers. Read cards aloud. No personal, family or faith disclosure is required.

title: Small actions that include people
objective: Use a scene card to identify an action that supports belonging.
source_label: CONSTRUCTED CLASSROOM SCENES — fictional examples. Background: the UN International Day of Peace is 21 September; this is a themed lesson, not a claim that today is that date.
source_lines: P1. At a fictional community workshop, Jo asks how to say a new participant’s name and then uses it correctly.
P2. A fictional club offers a written contribution as well as speaking, so a quiet participant can take part.
P3. Two fictional teams share a limited table by agreeing equal time slots.
P4. The actions can support respect, participation and fairness. We cannot know each person’s feelings from a short scene alone.
model: P2 offers more than one way to participate.
That action can help inclusion; the card does not prove how the participant feels.

hinge.question: What does P2 show?
choices: A. Everyone feels exactly the same.
B. A participant has a choice of response.
C. Speaking aloud is compulsory.
hinge.reason: The card offers writing or speaking; feelings are not reported.

task: Match P1, P2 and P3 to names / choice / fair sharing.
Choose a scene. Write the action and the value it may support.
Draft one fair instruction for the fictional workshop, based on a scene.
answers: P1 names; P2 choice; P3 fair sharing.
Example: equal time slots in P3 may support fairness.
Example: “You can write or speak.” Accept a feasible rule linked to the cards.
exit: Quietly write, draw or point to one action that may help someone join in.
misconception: Belonging is not proven by a photograph or imposed by compulsory public sharing. Keep examples fictional.
prep: Print the three scenes and response page. Quiet individual work is available throughout. No guided disclosure or public circle is needed.
access: Offer pointing, circling, drawing or scribed answers. Read cards aloud. No personal, family or faith disclosure is required.

subject: Humanities
title: A place in the group
objective: Explain how a group can help someone belong.
source_label: CONSTRUCTED TEACHING SOURCE: fictional classroom example, not an archival original.
source_lines: The fictional River Team looks after a garden.
Members choose a job: water, label or tidy.
A new member may watch before joining in.
The team thanks each contribution.
model: Choosing a job gives the new member a way to join.
Watching first is also an allowed choice.

hinge.question: Which action helps a new member belong?
choices: A. Force them to speak.
B. Offer a job or time to watch.
C. Ignore their contribution.
hinge.reason: A choice gives a safe way to take part without pressure.

task: Name the group and one thing it does.
Match two actions to belonging: offers a choice; thanks a contribution.
Create a group page: name, shared purpose, one welcome action. Use the fictional group or a chosen example.
answers: River Team; looks after a garden.
Both can show belonging; accept a clear explanation.
Accept a name, purpose and reasonable welcome action; no private details needed.
exit: One action that helps someone belong.

title: An object and its meaning
objective: Describe an object and explain a meaning using its card.
source_label: CONSTRUCTED CLASSROOM OBJECT CARDS — all people and objects below are fictional. Pupils may use these cards rather than personal belongings.
source_lines: S1. A blue fabric badge has a white wave and two stitched lines. In this fictional club it marks a shared river-cleaning project.
S2. A small red paper lamp has a yellow paper flame. In this fictional exhibition it helps visitors learn about using light as a symbol.
S3. A round cardboard token has a green tree. A fictional reading group uses it to mark finishing a shared book.
S4. Visible features can be described. A meaning needs a label or an explanation; appearance alone does not prove it.
model: I choose S1. I can describe its blue cloth, white wave and stitching.
Its card links it with a river-cleaning project; I do not need to invent a personal story.

hinge.question: What can we learn from an unlabelled object’s appearance alone?
choices: A. Every feeling of its owner.
B. Visible features, but not all its meanings.
C. The owner’s faith.
hinge.reason: S4 separates observation from an interpretation that needs evidence.

task: Choose S1, S2 or S3. Record three visible features from its description.
Add the meaning stated on its card and the card number.
Prepare a two-sentence museum label. Share it aloud, in writing or with an adult.
answers: S1: blue, fabric, white wave/two stitched lines. S2: small, red, paper/yellow paper flame. S3: round, cardboard, green tree.
Use the chosen card’s project, exhibition or reading-group meaning.
Example: “This blue fabric badge has a white wave. S1 says it marks a shared river-cleaning project.”
exit: What is one thing a label tells us that appearance might not?
misconception: An object can matter without being expensive. Sharing personal belongings, family experiences or beliefs is optional, never the assessment requirement.
prep: Print the fictional cards. No objects from home or special handling box are needed; allow a drawing or adult-read label.
access: Offer pointing, circling, drawing or scribed answers. Read cards aloud. No personal, family or faith disclosure is required.

subject: Humanities
title: Why move? What changes?
objective: Distinguish a reason for moving from a consequence.
source_label: CONSTRUCTED TEACHING SOURCE: fictional classroom example, not an archival original.
source_lines: Fictional case: Sam moves to a new town to start an offered job.
After the move, Sam uses a new bus route and meets new colleagues.
Sam still keeps in contact with old friends.
This case illustrates a possible experience, not every migrant's experience.
model: Cause: the offered job helps explain why Sam moved.
Consequence: the new bus route happens after the move.

hinge.question: Which is a cause in this case?
choices: A. Meeting new colleagues.
B. Using a new bus route.
C. The offered job.
hinge.reason: The job helps explain the move; the other details follow it.

task: Sort job, new bus route, new colleagues and old friends into cause, consequence or continuity.
Write: Sam moved because ___. As a result, ___.
Give one reason this case cannot explain every person's move.
answers: Cause: offered job. Consequences: new bus route/new colleagues. Continuity: old friends.
Job; new bus route or colleagues, linked accurately.
People move for different or multiple reasons; one fictional case is not evidence of everyone.
exit: A cause explains why. A consequence explains what followed.
misconception: Order alone does not prove causation. Avoid a single-reason story about all migration.
prep: Print the matching pupil sheets. Provide pencils and coloured pencils; pointing or adult scribing is available.

title: Diwali: the lamp and its meaning
objective: Explain a Diwali practice using evidence from a named source.
source_label: CLASSROOM FACT CARD — paraphrased from Hindu American Foundation. One introductory Hindu perspective; celebrations and stories vary.
source_lines: D1. Diwali is a Hindu festival commonly associated with light.
D2. Many celebrants use small clay oil lamps called diyas.
D3. The source connects the lamps with knowledge overcoming ignorance and good overcoming evil.
D4. A diagram of a diya shows an object. The written source helps us explain its meaning.
model: Practice: lighting diyas (D2).
Meaning: the source connects the light with knowledge and good (D3).

hinge.question: Which answer explains rather than only names the object?
choices: A. A diya is small.
B. The light represents knowledge overcoming ignorance in this source.
C. Every family celebrates identically.
hinge.reason: It gives a source-based meaning; A only describes and C overgeneralises.

task: Label practice / object / meaning using D1–D3.
Write two sentences linking a diya to its meaning. Include a line number.
Repair: “A picture proves what every Hindu believes.” Use D4.
answers: Practice: celebrating with light; object: diya; meaning: knowledge/good overcoming ignorance/evil.
Example: “Many celebrants use diyas (D2). The source links their light with knowledge overcoming ignorance (D3).”
A picture can show an object; a source is needed for its meaning, and one source does not represent everybody.
exit: Give one accurate practice-and-meaning link with a line number.
misconception: Light is not evidence that every festival tells the same story. Report the named source rather than assigning beliefs to classmates.
prep: Print the numbered fact card and response page. Draw an unlit diya if useful. No flames, food, video or external cards required.
access: Offer pointing, circling, drawing or scribed answers. Read cards aloud. No personal, family or faith disclosure is required.

subject: Humanities
title: Whose history is included?
objective: Use a named example to explain a contribution to British history.
source_label: SECONDARY TEACHING SUMMARY: paraphrased from The National Archives and UK Parliament.
source_lines: A. In 1948, Empire Windrush brought passengers from the Caribbean to Britain.
B. In 1963, Bristol campaigners opposed a bus company's racial discrimination.
C. Paul Stephenson and other organisers helped lead that campaign.
D. The 1965 Race Relations Act prohibited racial discrimination in some public places.
model: I choose B and C: campaigners challenged an unfair employment policy.
I name the action and the evidence, rather than only saying someone was famous.

hinge.question: Which is the strongest evidence-based statement?
choices: A. One person changed everything.
B. Bristol campaigners challenged racial discrimination in 1963.
C. Britain had no Black history before 1948.
hinge.reason: It names an action and a date supported by the source card.

task: Put A, B and D in date order.
Explain one contribution of the Bristol campaigners.
Write one question the summary does not answer.
answers: They organised opposition to the discriminatory bus policy; give B or C as evidence.
Accept who else organised, how individuals felt, the campaign's daily events, or another genuine gap.
exit: Name the contribution and the supporting detail.
misconception: Black British history did not begin in 1948. Avoid reducing a collective campaign to one hero.
prep: Print the matching pupil sheets. Provide pencils and coloured pencils; pointing or adult scribing is available.

title: Hanukkah: light and story
objective: Link a Hanukkah lighting practice to its remembered story.
source_label: CLASSROOM FACT CARD — paraphrased from Chabad.org. Reported Jewish tradition; the miracle is presented as a belief/story, not a classroom science finding.
source_lines: H1. Hanukkah is a Jewish festival lasting eight days. It recalls the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem.
H2. In the traditional account, oil expected to last one day lasts eight days.
H3. A hanukkiah has eight festival lights and a separate helper light, the shamash.
H4. One festival light is added each night; the eight lights recall the miracle. The helper is not a ninth festival night.
model: H3 gives eight festival lights plus one helper.
H2 and H4 explain why eight nights matter in the traditional account.

hinge.question: Why can a hanukkiah have nine light positions during an eight-day festival?
choices: A. The festival actually lasts nine days.
B. One position holds the helper light.
C. One position is a mistake.
hinge.reason: H3 distinguishes eight festival lights from the shamash.

task: Draw and label eight festival-light positions plus one separate helper position.
Match story / object / practice to H2, H3 and H4.
Explain why adding lights is more than decoration in this source.
answers: Eight festival positions and a clearly labelled helper; do not count the helper as an extra night.
Story H2; object H3; practice H4.
The lights recall the traditional miracle of oil lasting eight days (H2/H4).
exit: Explain the difference between the eight lights and the helper.
misconception: The Temple menorah and the Hanukkah lamp are not interchangeable diagrams. Draw the nine-position hanukkiah required by this card.
prep: Use the printed fact card and a drawn lamp. No lighting ceremony, flame or personal-faith disclosure is required.
access: Offer pointing, circling, drawing or scribed answers. Read cards aloud. No personal, family or faith disclosure is required.

subject: Humanities
title: Why was it significant?
objective: Judge significance using a reason and evidence.
source_label: SECONDARY TEACHING SUMMARY: The National Archives and UK Parliament.
source_lines: A. In 1948, Empire Windrush brought passengers from the Caribbean to Britain.
B. In 1963, Bristol campaigners opposed a bus company's racial discrimination.
C. Paul Stephenson and other organisers helped lead that campaign.
D. The 1965 Race Relations Act prohibited racial discrimination in some public places.
model: A campaign can matter because it challenges a barrier affecting people.
I still need evidence of what changed and who was affected. Fame alone is not enough.

hinge.question: Which reason explains historical significance?
choices: A. A person is well known.
B. An action challenged unfair treatment.
C. A name is easy to remember.
hinge.reason: It explains an impact, rather than popularity.

task: Choose a person or event from the evidence card.
Explain why it mattered using one labelled detail.
State what further evidence would strengthen your judgement.
answers: Accept 1963 campaign/Paul Stephenson/1965 Act.
Example: The campaign mattered because it challenged racial discrimination; B supports this.
An account of the outcome, people affected, later change or another relevant source.
exit: It mattered because ___. The evidence is ___.
misconception: The 1965 Act did not end racism or ban all discrimination in every area. Significance needs a specific criterion.

title: Christmas: belief and symbol
objective: Explain how a Christmas symbol links to Christian belief.
source_label: CLASSROOM FACT CARDS — paraphrases of Church of England teaching and worship. These are teaching summaries, not quotations or a complete nativity story.
source_lines: C1. Christians celebrate the birth of Jesus at Christmas.
C2. Church of England teaching describes Jesus’ birth as a gift from God.
C3. In Church of England Christmas worship, a candle may accompany the description of Jesus as the light of the world.
C4. A candle is the visible object. Its Christian meaning comes from the words and belief, not from wax alone.
model: C1 gives the belief being remembered: Jesus’ birth.
C3 links a visible candle with a Christian description of Jesus.

hinge.question: Which statement best separates object from meaning?
choices: A. Wax itself tells the whole belief.
B. A candle may express belief about Jesus; the source explains this.
C. Everyone who sees a candle is Christian.
hinge.reason: C3–C4 link the symbol to a source without assigning a belief to everyone.

task: Match birth / gift / light to C1, C2 or C3.
Write two linked sentences: what is celebrated, and what the candle can represent.
Explain why a shop-window candle alone cannot establish somebody’s belief.
answers: Birth C1; gift C2; light C3.
Christians celebrate Jesus’ birth; in this worship source a candle accompanies Jesus as light of the world.
The same object can be used in different settings; we need the context or an explanation.
exit: Name a Christmas belief and the line that supports it.
misconception: Do not treat all Christmas customs as religious, or ask pupils to describe their own celebrations. These cards are not four Gospel accounts.
prep: Print the four lines and response page. Use a paper candle diagram only; a nativity model, video or celebration activity is unnecessary.
access: Offer pointing, circling, drawing or scribed answers. Read cards aloud. No personal, family or faith disclosure is required.

subject: Humanities
title: Plan an account
objective: Select and organise relevant evidence before writing.
source_label: SECONDARY TEACHING SUMMARY: The National Archives and UK Parliament.
source_lines: A. In 1948, Empire Windrush brought passengers from the Caribbean to Britain.
B. In 1963, Bristol campaigners opposed a bus company's racial discrimination.
C. Paul Stephenson and other organisers helped lead that campaign.
D. The 1965 Race Relations Act prohibited racial discrimination in some public places.
model: Question: How did people challenge unfair treatment in Britain?
Choose B and C for the campaign; D helps show later legal change. A needs an explained link.

hinge.question: Which plan best answers the question?
choices: A. List every fact without links.
B. Make a claim, select evidence, explain the link.
C. Write only a favourite fact.
hinge.reason: Selection and explanation make the answer relevant.

task: Write one sentence answering the question.
Choose two evidence details and explain how each helps.
Plan an ending that answers the question again.
answers: Accept people organised campaigns and pressed for change.
B/C: collective protest against discrimination. D: legal response in 1965; do not claim the boycott was the only cause.
A reasoned answer using the selected evidence, with no claim that all unfairness ended.
exit: Which detail did you choose, and why?
misconception: A list is not an explanation. Do not turn a sequence into a claim that one event was the sole cause.
prep: Print the matching pupil sheets. Provide pencils and coloured pencils; pointing or adult scribing is available.

title: Compare festivals of light
objective: Write one supported similarity and one supported difference.
source_label: CLASSROOM COMPARISON CARDS — concise paraphrases of Hindu American Foundation and Chabad.org; retain each source’s identity.
source_lines: D1. In this Hindu account of Diwali, diyas connect light with good overcoming evil and knowledge overcoming ignorance.
H1. In this Jewish account of Hanukkah, an added light each night recalls the traditional miracle of oil lasting eight days.
V1. Both accounts link light with religious meaning.
V2. Similar objects do not establish identical stories, beliefs or practices.
model: Both accounts give light a religious meaning (D1/H1).
Their explanations differ: Diwali’s stated theme and Hanukkah’s remembered oil story.

hinge.question: Which comparison is supported?
choices: A. Both use meaningful light, with different explanations.
B. Hanukkah is simply another name for Diwali.
C. The brightest display has the best belief.
hinge.reason: It identifies a similarity while retaining the sources’ different meanings.

task: Complete two rows: festival / source’s meaning / supporting line.
Write one “Both…” sentence and one “Whereas…” sentence.
Repair “All festivals of light are identical.” Use evidence from both cards.
answers: Diwali: good/knowledge overcoming evil/ignorance, D1. Hanukkah: the oil miracle, H1.
Both link light with meaning. Diwali’s card emphasises good/knowledge, whereas Hanukkah’s recalls the oil story.
Both use light, but D1 and H1 give different explanations; similarity is not identity.
exit: Give a difference without a ranking word such as better or worse.
misconception: A respectful comparison can name real differences. Respect does not require claiming every tradition is the same.
prep: Print the two main source cards and comparison grid. Keep previous weeks’ references available for David; no internet required to answer.
access: Offer pointing, circling, drawing or scribed answers. Read cards aloud. No personal, family or faith disclosure is required.

subject: Humanities
title: Write and check an account
objective: Write an evidence-based account and evaluate its source.
source_label: SECONDARY TEACHING SUMMARY: The National Archives and UK Parliament.
source_lines: A. In 1948, Empire Windrush brought passengers from the Caribbean to Britain.
B. In 1963, Bristol campaigners opposed a bus company's racial discrimination.
C. Paul Stephenson and other organisers helped lead that campaign.
D. The 1965 Race Relations Act prohibited racial discrimination in some public places.
model: Today's question: How did people challenge unfair treatment in Britain?
Use a claim, two evidence details and a conclusion. Keep the source's limits visible.

hinge.question: What should a source evaluation include?
choices: A. Useful for this question, with a reason and a limit.
B. It is online, so it must be true.
C. It is short, so it is useless.
hinge.reason: Usefulness depends on the question and the content/provenance.

task: Write an account answering the question with two facts.
Evaluate the card: useful for ___ because ___; it cannot tell me ___.
Check one sentence and record one improvement after your first attempt.
answers: Accept a clear account using the 1963 campaign and/or 1965 Act, with accurate links.
Useful for key events/dates; cannot provide all participants' voices or explain every cause.
Accept a specific change: add evidence, correct a date, qualify an overclaim or improve a link.
exit: Keep the first attempt; name the next improvement.
misconception: This is a classroom assessment, not an awarding-body test or automatic UAS/PEQ sign-off.

title: Remembrance: report with care
objective: Use sources to explain remembrance, peace and freedom of choice.
source_label: CLASSROOM FACT CARDS — paraphrases of the Royal British Legion and United Nations. A themed reflection, not an assertion that the lesson date is an observance.
source_lines: R1. The Royal British Legion describes the red poppy as remembering service and sacrifice and expressing hope for peace.
R2. The Legion says wearing a poppy is a personal choice; people may remember in different ways.
U1. The UN International Day of Peace, on 21 September, promotes peace and non-violence.
U2. These are different observances. Their stated aims allow a comparison about peace, not a claim that they are identical.
model: R1 connects remembrance with hope for peace.
U1 concerns peace and non-violence; that gives a shared theme with a different focus.

hinge.question: Which conclusion respects both the evidence and choice?
choices: A. Everyone must wear a poppy.
B. All observances are identical.
C. People can value peace and choose different ways to remember.
hinge.reason: R2 explicitly permits choice; R1/U1 support the peace comparison.

task: Write a one-sentence report of R1 and a one-sentence report of U1.
Identify one shared aim and one difference in focus.
Repair “Not wearing a poppy proves disrespect.” Use R2.
answers: R1: the poppy remembers service/sacrifice and hope for peace. U1: the Day of Peace promotes peace/non-violence.
Shared aim: peace. Difference: R1 focuses on remembrance; U1 on a wider day for peace/non-violence.
The source says wearing one is a personal choice, so that conclusion is unsupported.
exit: Choose a source line. Explain one way to report its meaning without judging another person.
misconception: No compulsory silence, poppy wearing, bereavement account or family military-history disclosure. Offer a neutral source-analysis response.
prep: Print the cards and response page. Warn briefly that the topic includes remembrance; keep it non-graphic and offer quiet written work.
access: Offer pointing, circling, drawing or scribed answers. Read cards aloud. No personal, family or faith disclosure is required.

subject: Humanities / RE
title: What can a source prove?
objective: Evaluate an archive record and distinguish evidence from authority.
source_label: SECONDARY SOURCE CARD describing an archival original: The National Archives passenger list.
source_lines: Archive record: passenger list for Empire Windrush, arrival in Britain, June 1948.
A passenger list records details of passengers and a journey.
It does not, by itself, explain every passenger's motives or feelings.
Compare with another kind of source before making a wider claim.
model: Useful for a passenger or journey question: the record was made for the voyage.
Limited for a feelings question: administrative details are not a full personal account.

hinge.question: Which claim goes beyond the list?
choices: A. It records passengers.
B. It is linked to the 1948 journey.
C. Every passenger felt the same.
hinge.reason: A passenger list cannot establish everyone's feelings.

task: Record what the source is, when it was made and what it is useful for.
Write a judgement with one supported claim and one limit.
Name each source type. Explain how A1 and B1 could support a fair way for the fictional volunteer to contribute.
answers: Passenger list; 1948; useful for recorded passengers/journey details.
Accept a supported specific claim and a limit about motives, experiences or missing voices.

A1: Christian sacred text/Jesus’ teaching; fair treatment follows the stated reciprocal rule. B1: humanist ethical explanation; considering the volunteer’s experience and wellbeing can support inclusion. Application is our reasoned inference, not a reported event.
exit: Useful for what? What else would you need?
misconception: A primary source is not automatically complete or neutral. A belief source is not a passenger record.
prep: Print the matching pupil sheets. Provide pencils and coloured pencils; pointing or adult scribing is available.
re_source_lines: A1. Matthew 7:12 presents Jesus teaching people to treat others as they would wish to be treated. This is a paraphrase of a Christian sacred text.
B1. Humanists UK describes ethical decisions using reason, empathy and concern for wellbeing. This is a summary from a non-religious organisation.
F1. Fictional application: a community display team decides whether a new volunteer should have a way to contribute.
re_source_label: CLASSROOM SOURCE SUMMARIES — paraphrases or explicitly labelled fictional applications; not quotations. Use within the one 40-minute Humanities/RE lesson.
re_objective: Identify two sources of authority and explain one meaning from each.

subject: Humanities / RE
title: A timeline with a reason
objective: Order events and explain a change while comparing shared values.
source_label: SECONDARY TEACHING SUMMARY: The National Archives and UK Parliament.
source_lines: A. In 1948, Empire Windrush brought passengers from the Caribbean to Britain.
B. In 1963, Bristol campaigners opposed a bus company's racial discrimination.
C. Paul Stephenson and other organisers helped lead that campaign.
D. The 1965 Race Relations Act prohibited racial discrimination in some public places.
model: Put events in chronological order; add a reason each event matters.
A gap between our selected events does not prove that nothing happened.

hinge.question: What does a gap between our selected dates prove?
choices: A. Nothing changed.
B. Our selection contains no event there.
C. Everyone agreed.
hinge.reason: A selected timeline is incomplete; gaps are not evidence of no change.

task: Order 1948, 1963 and 1965; add a description to each.
Choose one change and justify its place on the timeline.
Write one shared value and explain how each source could support the fictional event’s aim.
answers: 1948 Windrush; 1963 Bristol campaign; 1965 Race Relations Act.
Accept supported campaign/legal change; avoid claiming all racism ended.

Peace is a defensible shared aim in this application. A1 can guide a Christian through Jesus’ teaching; B1 can guide a humanist through concern for experiences and consequences. Do not claim the sources prove every believer attends the Day of Peace.
exit: One event, one reason, one limit of this timeline.
misconception: Time gaps do not prove continuity. Shared values do not mean identical beliefs.
prep: Print the matching pupil sheets. Provide pencils and coloured pencils; pointing or adult scribing is available.
re_source_lines: A1. Matthew 5:9 presents Jesus praising peacemakers. This paraphrase is from a Christian sacred text.
B1. Humanists UK explains that empathy and experience can guide decisions. This is a non-religious ethical approach.
U1. The UN Day of Peace is 21 September. A fictional community event asks visitors to solve disagreements without violence.
re_source_label: CLASSROOM SOURCE SUMMARIES — paraphrases or explicitly labelled fictional applications; not quotations. Use within the one 40-minute Humanities/RE lesson.
re_objective: Compare a religious and non-religious reason for peaceful action.

subject: Humanities / RE
title: People, action and impact
objective: Explain historical significance and connect an action to a stated value.
source_label: SECONDARY TEACHING SUMMARY: UK Parliament; values discussion is a classroom interpretation.
source_lines: A. In 1948, Empire Windrush brought passengers from the Caribbean to Britain.
B. In 1963, Bristol campaigners opposed a bus company's racial discrimination.
C. Paul Stephenson and other organisers helped lead that campaign.
D. The 1965 Race Relations Act prohibited racial discrimination in some public places.
model: Paul Stephenson worked with other campaigners in Bristol.
A strong explanation links a named action, evidence and an impact; it does not assume private beliefs.

hinge.question: Which statement avoids an unsupported claim?
choices: A. We know every organiser's religion.
B. Campaigners challenged an unfair policy.
C. One campaign ended all racism.
hinge.reason: The card supports their action; it does not establish every belief or every later outcome.

task: Explain the significance of the Bristol campaign using two facts.
Write a second possible judgement or a limitation.
Write two developed points: source idea → possible action → why the link makes sense. Label possible actions as inferences.
answers: Accept the 1963 challenge to discriminatory employment and collective organising; link action and barrier.
Need evidence of outcomes/long-term impact; other campaigns and causes also mattered.

Example: A Christian volunteer could connect receiving a gift with giving welcome; that is an interpretation grounded in A1. A humanist volunteer could connect assistance with improving people’s lives, grounded in B1. Other reasoned links are valid; shared action need not mean identical belief.
exit: Explain an action without inventing a belief.
misconception: Significance differs from fame. Never infer a person's religion from their name or heritage.
prep: Print the matching pupil sheets. Provide pencils and coloured pencils; pointing or adult scribing is available.
re_source_lines: A1. At Christmas Christians celebrate Jesus’ birth; Church of England teaching describes it as God’s gift.
B1. Humanists UK describes helping others to find wellbeing and meaning in this life.
F1. Fictional application: two volunteers support a community welcome event, each drawing on a different source.
re_source_label: CLASSROOM SOURCE SUMMARIES — paraphrases or explicitly labelled fictional applications; not quotations. Use within the one 40-minute Humanities/RE lesson.
re_objective: Make two developed points linking a belief or value to an action.

subject: Humanities / RE
title: An account with evidence
objective: Write a connected account and explain a viewpoint on peace.
source_label: SECONDARY TEACHING SUMMARY: The National Archives and UK Parliament.
source_lines: A. In 1948, Empire Windrush brought passengers from the Caribbean to Britain.
B. In 1963, Bristol campaigners opposed a bus company's racial discrimination.
C. Paul Stephenson and other organisers helped lead that campaign.
D. The 1965 Race Relations Act prohibited racial discrimination in some public places.
model: Question: How did people challenge unfair treatment in Britain?
Use a claim, selected evidence and explanation. Qualify claims that go beyond the sources.

hinge.question: Which ending is defensible?
choices: A. All unfairness ended in 1965.
B. Campaigns and legal change challenged some barriers.
C. Only one person acted.
hinge.reason: It fits the evidence and avoids total or single-cause claims.

task: Write two connected paragraphs answering the question.
Add a source judgement: usefulness and limitation.
Using A1 and B1, suggest two different reasons for peaceful action. Use R1 to explain why this does not require identical remembrance practices.
answers: Accept campaign and legal change with dates and explained links.
The summaries identify key events; need more primary voices and outcome evidence.

A1 offers a religious reason through Jesus’ teaching; B1 offers a non-religious reason through people’s experiences and effects on wellbeing. R1 makes poppy wearing a choice. These sources do not establish how every member of a group observes remembrance.
exit: Which claim is strongest, and what supports it?
misconception: Remembering is not the same as celebrating conflict. No personal bereavement disclosure is required.
prep: Print the matching pupil sheets. Provide pencils and coloured pencils; pointing or adult scribing is available.
re_source_lines: R1. The Royal British Legion links remembrance with hope for peace and says wearing a poppy is a choice.
A1. Matthew 5:9 presents Jesus praising people who make peace.
B1. Humanist ethical thinking can use empathy and experience to consider how actions affect others.
re_source_label: CLASSROOM SOURCE SUMMARIES — paraphrases or explicitly labelled fictional applications; not quotations. Use within the one 40-minute Humanities/RE lesson.

subject: Humanities / RE
title: Two enquiries, clear evidence
objective: Complete a source judgement and a reasoned belief-and-identity response.
source_label: SECONDARY TEACHING SUMMARY: The National Archives and UK Parliament.
source_lines: A. In 1948, Empire Windrush brought passengers from the Caribbean to Britain.
B. In 1963, Bristol campaigners opposed a bus company's racial discrimination.
C. Paul Stephenson and other organisers helped lead that campaign.
D. The 1965 Race Relations Act prohibited racial discrimination in some public places.
model: Section A: How did people challenge unfair treatment in Britain?
Section B: How can values shape belonging? Use a stated example, not a guess about someone.

hinge.question: Which response respects the evidence?
choices: A. Everyone in a group thinks alike.
B. A stated value can guide an action; people within groups differ.
C. Identity tells us all someone's beliefs.
hinge.reason: A reasoned example does not erase variation within groups.

task: Write a short historical account answering the question with two source details.
Evaluate the history card: one use for this question and one limitation.
Name both sources, give one accurate idea from each, and evaluate F1. Finish with one way a value might influence a voluntary action.
answers: Credit an accurate claim, two facts and reasoned links about campaigns or legal change.
Useful for key events and dates; limited for participants’ voices, every cause and the full impact. Link the judgement to the historical question.

A1 identifies a religious source; B1 a non-religious one. The same action does not establish identical belief. Credit accurate source identification, supported comparison and a clearly signalled inference; do not demand personal-faith disclosure.
exit: Keep both enquiry responses and one next step.
misconception: Split the 40 minutes across both outcomes. This is curriculum evidence, not an external qualification result.
prep: Print the matching pupil sheets. Provide pencils and coloured pencils; pointing or adult scribing is available.
re_source_lines: A1. In a Christian Christmas source, Jesus’ birth is described as a gift from God.
B1. In a humanist source, meaning can be developed through this life and concern for others.
F1. Fictional claim to evaluate: “Two volunteers help at the same project, so their beliefs must be identical.”
re_source_label: CLASSROOM SOURCE SUMMARIES — paraphrases or explicitly labelled fictional applications; not quotations. Use within the one 40-minute Humanities/RE lesson.
re_objective: Independently compare two sources and separate evidence from inference.
